idiom_name: by-value operator= plus a noexcept member/friend swap (unifying assignment operator)
implementation_notes: Since C++11 the whole idiom is a by-value parameter and a swap: T& operator=(T other) { swap(other); return *this; } -- the copy from an lvalue or the move from an rvalue is performed at the call site, before the body runs, so if constructing the argument throws, the operator was never entered and *this is untouched. Only a member-wise exchange that cannot throw remains in the body (mark it noexcept and keep every member swap inside the same guarantee; std::is_nothrow_swappable is what the standard library queries before it moves your elements), and the parameter's destructor releases the old state on return, so self-assignment needs no check. Provide a member swap plus an ADL friend swap and express operator= in terms of them; where value-type members already copy and swap correctly, the rule of zero is the honest alternative to writing this at all.
pitfalls: A swap that can throw inside a noexcept assignment calls std::terminate; audit every member, including pre-C++11 types whose swap has no noexcept specification -- one non-noexcept member swap poisons the whole chain.

The by-value parameter is both copy and move assignment, so no separate noexcept move-assign exists: a type with an expensive destructor pays for destroying the temporary, and is_nothrow_copy_assignable stays false even though operator= is noexcept.

The idiom always reallocates the target's resources, so it is the wrong tool for a hot-path assignment that could reuse storage, and it does not apply to types owning a std::mutex or std::atomic member, which cannot be swapped.

variants.name: const& operator= with an explicit local temporary (C++98)
variants.idiom_name: const& operator= plus a throw()-qualified swap with an explicit temporary
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11 the temporary is created explicitly inside a const-reference overload: T& operator=(const T& rhs) { T tmp(rhs); swap(tmp); return *this; }. Copy elision does not apply to a const reference bound to an rvalue, so assigning from a temporary costs an extra copy-construction and destruction compared with the by-value form -- that is exactly the refinement the idiom gained with move semantics and elision. Exception specifications are spelled throw() rather than noexcept, there is no move-assignment path, and the self-assignment check the by-value form obviates is often kept. Choose this form only for C++98/03 toolchains or code that must stay source-compatible with them.
pitfalls: Without move semantics or elision the rvalue path really does copy, so the explicit temporary survives on C++98 compilers instead of being replaced by the by-value parameter.
throw() must genuinely hold: on those compilers a throw escaping swap calls std::terminate, and the era's compilers did not diagnose a missing or wrong specification.
The const-reference signature blocks adding a move-assignment later without changing overload behaviour, so migrating to the by-value form is a deliberate, tested change rather than a local edit.
